opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back. The biggest change is that the field has gone from being very speculative to being much more concrete. When I first got interested in AI risk, much of the work was abstract. People were trying to reason about systems that didn't exist yet, and it was hard to know whether you were making progress or what a good project even looked like. That made it a tough area to recommend to most people, because you needed an unusual temperament to sit with that much uncertainty and still be productive.

Now we have very capable models that people can study, poke at, and run experiments on. If you care about whether AI systems might deceive their developers, or whether we can tell what they're "thinking," or whether dangerous capabilities are emerging, you can design an experiment and get real data. Interpretability, evaluations, control, and alignment research have all become much more empirical, and that opens the door to many more people. Good engineers, people with ordinary research skills, and people who are good at running organizations can now contribute directly.

The second big change is that the world is paying attention. Governments, AI companies, and the broader public take the topic seriously in a way they didn't a few years ago. So there are many more jobs, more funding, and more real decision points. Policy work is a good example. There are concrete questions being decided right now about evaluations, security standards, and what companies should commit to, and having thoughtful people in those rooms can matter a lot.

The third thing is that I think the stakes feel more pressing. My view is that transformative AI could plausibly arrive within a timeframe that matters for people's careers today. That makes being early to this field much more valuable than it might be in a slower world.

I'd add a caveat, though. "Better area to work in" doesn't mean easy or that every job labeled "AI safety" is valuable. There's a real risk of people doing work that mostly accelerates capabilities while telling themselves it's safety work, or of joining something without thinking hard about its impact. So I'd encourage people to be thoughtful about where they go. But overall, the number of ways for a person with a wide range of skills to help has gone up enormously, and that's the main reason I'm more enthusiastic than I used to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI work has become more empirical, with experiments producing real data that make progress easier to assess, and that there are now many more jobs. It presents both as reasons the field is better to work in.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the short version is that there's just a lot more to do now, and a lot more of it is concrete.

When I first started thinking seriously about this, maybe ten or fifteen years ago, the case for working on AI was almost entirely theoretical. You had a small number of people saying, "Look, if we ever build systems that are smarter than us, that could go very badly, and we should think about that." And I think that argument was basically right. But the actual work you could do was pretty limited. It was a lot of philosophy, a lot of thought experiments, a lot of trying to reason about systems that didn't exist yet. And it was hard to know whether anything you were doing was actually making a difference, because the thing you were worried about was so far away and so abstract.

What's changed is that the systems are here now. They're not the fully transformative systems that I think are still coming, but they're real, they're capable, they're being deployed at enormous scale, and they're exhibiting a lot of the properties people were worried about in a kind of early, manageable form. So you can actually study them. You can run experiments on alignment. You can test whether your interpretability tools work. You can look at how a model behaves when you try to get it to deceive you, and you learn something real. That's a completely different situation from where we were.

And then on the policy and governance side, it's gone from being something that nobody in government would take a meeting about to being something that heads of state talk about. There are actual institutions, actual regulatory conversations, actual companies with safety teams and responsible scaling policies, however imperfect those are. So if you want to work on governance, there's now a there there. You're not just writing papers hoping someone reads them.

I'd also say the field has gotten more legible. It used to be that if you wanted to contribute, you kind of had to find your way into a very small community and figure out what was going on through conversations. Now there are research agendas, there are organizations with job openings, there are well-defined problems that a smart person can pick up and make progress on. That lowers the barrier a lot.

And I think the last thing, which is maybe less obvious, is that the stakes have become clearer to a lot more people. I don't think you have to buy into any particularly exotic view to think that AI is going to be one of the most important things that happens this century. So the pool of people who want to help is bigger, the pool of funders is bigger, and the number of ways to plug in is bigger.

The flip side, and I want to be honest about this, is that it's also gotten more crowded and more contested. There's a lot of money in it now, a lot of commercial pressure, and that creates its own problems. Some of the work is less neglected than it was. But on net, I think if you're someone trying to figure out where you can make a real difference on this, your options are much better than they were, and the feedback loops are much tighter. You can actually tell whether you're helping. That's a big deal.

r001.rationale: The response says there are organizations with job openings and well-defined problems, and that tighter feedback loops make it possible to tell whether your work is helping.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that the opportunities to do useful work have become much more concrete. You used to have to buy a fairly abstract argument: AI could eventually be enormously important, and perhaps there are things we should do now to make that go well. But it was hard to say exactly what those things were, or how you’d know whether you were making progress.

Now you can work with actual systems and ask: What can they do? Where do they fail? Can we understand why they behave the way they do? Can we make them more reliable? That gives you much more of a feedback loop, and it opens up the area to people with a wider range of skills.

There’s also more reason to think the decisions being made today could matter a lot. You don’t have to be confident about exactly when very powerful AI will arrive to think it’s worth having good people working on how to evaluate it and how to manage its risks.

So I’d distinguish ‘this is an important problem’ from ‘this is a good area for someone to enter.’ I’ve thought the first for a long time. What’s changed is that there are more concrete ways to contribute, learn, and find out whether you’re actually helping.

r001.rationale: The response says useful work in AI has become more concrete, with a stronger feedback loop for assessing progress and whether one is helping, making it a better area to enter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that there are now more concrete things to do. For a long time, if you were worried about very powerful AI, you had this problem where the systems you were worried about didn’t exist yet. So you were trying to figure out, pretty abstractly, what could go wrong and what research today might help with that. That’s a hard thing to make progress on, and it’s also hard to tell whether you’re making progress.

As AI systems have become more capable, there’s more opportunity to study their behavior directly, try ways of making them safer, and get feedback from experiments. There are also more concrete decisions for companies and governments to make. You don’t have to resolve every question about the distant future to help people make those decisions better.

That doesn’t mean the work is easy, or that every project with ‘AI safety’ in the title is useful. But I think there’s a broader range of ways to contribute, and a better chance of finding work where you can explain what you’re doing, why it matters, and what would count as progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes more concrete ways to contribute and feedback from experiments, but it does not clearly identify the availability of AI jobs with feedback on whether the work succeeds as the reason.
